Active Devices, Power Supplies, and Amplifiers

Unit 2: Fundamentals of Electricity and Electronics. Lesson 11 of 60 in CBET Academy.

Active devices control or amplify. They are what turn wall power into the clean rails a device needs and turn a microvolt heart signal into a waveform on a screen.

Diodes

A diode conducts in one direction only, dropping about 0.7 V (silicon) when it does. Uses: rectifiers turn AC into pulsing DC (half-wave uses one diode, full-wave two, a bridge four); a zener diode conducts backward at a fixed voltage and holds a reference; an LED emits light and is the source in pulse oximeter probes.

The power supply, stage by stage

  1. Transformer steps the mains down (or a switching stage chops it at high frequency).
  2. Rectifier turns AC into pulsing DC.
  3. Filter capacitor smooths the pulses; too little capacitance or a dried-out capacitor leaves ripple.
  4. Regulator holds the output steady as load and input vary.

Linear supplies are simple and quiet but heavy and inefficient, wasting the difference as heat. Switching supplies chop the input at tens of kilohertz, are light and efficient, and are in nearly every modern device; they are noisier and many need a minimum load to regulate. Most supply faults are failed capacitors, blown fuses from a shorted downstream component, or a regulator that drifts.

Transistors and thyristors

A transistor (NPN or PNP) uses a small base current to control a larger collector-emitter current: a switch or an amplifier. SCRs and triacs switch large AC loads such as motors and heaters. Failed transistors usually short.

Operational amplifiers

An op-amp has very high gain, and with feedback it follows two rules: the inputs draw no current, and the output does whatever it takes to make the two inputs equal. Resistor ratios set the gain. Inverting and non-inverting configurations amplify; a differential or instrumentation amplifier amplifies the difference between two inputs and rejects what they have in common. That common-mode rejection (CMRR) is why an ECG front end can pull a 1 mV heart signal out of volts of 60 Hz interference on both electrodes.

Isolation

Patient-connected circuits float from ground so leakage current cannot reach the patient. Optocouplers pass signals as light across a gap; isolation amplifiers and isolation transformers do the same for analog signals and power. A failed isolation barrier shows up as excess patient leakage on the safety analyzer.

From analog to digital

An analog-to-digital converter samples a signal and turns each sample into a number. Resolution in bits sets the steps: 8 bits is 256 levels, 12 bits is 4,096. Sample faster than twice the highest frequency of interest (the Nyquist rule) or the signal is misrepresented. A DAC does the reverse to drive displays and outputs.

Exam tip: rectifier then filter then regulator; ripple means a bad filter capacitor. An instrumentation amplifier with high CMRR rejects 60 Hz on ECG leads. Isolation keeps patient circuits floating; excess patient leakage points to the barrier.
Remember
Diode one way, 0.7 V; rectifier, filter capacitor, regulator; ripple means the capacitor. Linear quiet and heavy, switching efficient and noisy. Transistor is a switch or amplifier. Instrumentation amp with high CMRR for ECG. Optocouplers isolate. ADC resolution and Nyquist.
Deeper explanation

Active Devices, Power Supplies, and Amplifiers, explained slowly

The parts that do something

Passive parts shape energy; active parts control it. A diode decides direction, a transistor decides how much, an op-amp multiplies a whisper into a signal you can see. Every medical device is a power supply feeding amplifiers feeding a converter, and each stage fails in its own way.

Diodes: one-way valves

Current flows from anode to cathode (the direction of the arrow) and not backward, at a cost of about 0.7 V.

rectifier diode    turns AC into pulsing DC
zener              conducts backward at a fixed voltage; a cheap voltage reference and clamp
LED                emits light when conducting; the red and infrared sources in an oximeter probe

Rectifier arrangements: half-wave (one diode, uses half the cycle), full-wave (two diodes and a center-tapped transformer), bridge (four diodes, uses both halves, the common choice).

A power supply, stage by stage

mains --> [transformer] --> [rectifier] --> [filter capacitor] --> [regulator] --> clean DC rails
          steps down        AC to pulsing DC   smooths the pulses     holds voltage steady
          (or a high-frequency switching stage in a switching supply)

Where each stage fails and what you see:

transformer       open winding: no output at all; shorted turns: hot, low voltage, hum
rectifier diode   one shorted: blown fuse; one open: half the ripple frequency, low output
filter capacitor  dried out: ripple, hum in audio, random resets, low voltage under load, bulged top
regulator         drifted or failed: output too high (damages the load) or too low (resets); often runs hot
fuse              blown: usually a symptom of a short downstream, so find the short before replacing it

Linear supplies regulate by burning off the excess as heat: simple, quiet, heavy, inefficient. Switching supplies chop the input at tens of kilohertz through a small transformer and regulate by adjusting the duty cycle: light, efficient, and in nearly everything modern, but electrically noisy, and many will not regulate without a minimum load. Bench-test a switching supply with a load resistor, not open-circuit.

Transistors and thyristors

A transistor has three terminals. A small current into the base controls a large current between collector and emitter (NPN is the common type; PNP is its mirror). Two roles: a switch (fully on or off, as in a digital output or a motor driver) and an amplifier (partly on, proportionally). Transistors usually fail shorted; a shorted output transistor takes the fuse with it. SCRs and triacs switch heavy AC loads such as heaters and motors and are found in sterilizers, warmers, and centrifuges.

Op-amps: the universal amplifier

An operational amplifier has enormous gain and two inputs. With feedback it obeys two rules that let you predict any circuit:

  1. The inputs draw no current.
  2. The output does whatever is needed to make the two inputs equal.

Resistors around it set the gain: an inverting amplifier's gain is the feedback resistor over the input resistor.

The configuration that matters most in medicine is the differential amplifier, and its refined form, the instrumentation amplifier. It amplifies the difference between two inputs and ignores what they share.

electrode A:  1 mV heart signal  +  2 V of 60 Hz hum picked up from the room
electrode B:  0 mV (reference)   +  2 V of the SAME 60 Hz hum
difference:   1 mV heart signal  +  0 V hum          the hum cancels; the heart signal survives

How well it cancels is the common-mode rejection ratio. A high CMRR is why an ECG front end can display microvolts in a room full of interference. The right-leg electrode drives the patient's common-mode voltage back toward the amplifier's reference to improve it further.

Isolation: keeping the patient floating

Patient-connected inputs must never provide a path for leakage or fault current. The signal crosses an isolation barrier: an optocoupler turns the signal into light across a gap and back; an isolation amplifier does the same for analog signals; an isolation transformer does it for power. If the barrier degrades, the safety analyzer shows rising patient leakage, and that is the clue.

Analog to digital

The waveform must become numbers.

resolution   8 bits = 256 levels, 10 bits = 1024, 12 bits = 4096, 16 bits = 65,536    finer steps
sampling     at least twice the highest frequency of interest (Nyquist); ECG at 150 Hz diagnostic bandwidth
             needs well over 300 samples per second, so 500 to 1000 is typical
aliasing     sample too slowly and a fast signal masquerades as a slow one

A DAC reverses the process for outputs such as pacing pulses and display drives.

How the exam asks it

  • "Which power supply stage converts AC to DC?" The rectifier.
  • "A monitor resets randomly and the supply output shows ripple; which component?" The filter capacitor.
  • "Which amplifier characteristic allows an ECG to reject 60 Hz interference?" High common-mode rejection ratio.
  • "What component provides electrical isolation between the patient and the mains?" An optocoupler or isolation amplifier.
  • "Minimum sampling rate for a 100 Hz signal?" More than 200 samples per second.

What to memorize

  • Diode 0.7 V, one way; bridge rectifier; transformer, rectifier, filter, regulator.
  • Ripple means the capacitor; blown fuse means find the short; switching supplies need a load.
  • Instrumentation amplifier with high CMRR rejects hum. Optocouplers isolate. Nyquist: sample above twice the highest frequency.
